For the last two decades, more and more elements have been replaced or extended with the help of technological tools. Technology offers incredible possibilities, new ways to improve processes, interactions, and experiences. My vision as a designer is to implement technology meaningfully, rather than throwing it at a problem. An example is the current trend of embedding AI everywhere, without considering the consequences it brings along \cite{zhai2024}. A term that aptly describes this is 'Techno-Solutionism' \cite{mitra2023}, the belief that technology alone can solve all problems. This mindset risks reducing complex societal challenges to purely technical problems, overlooking their social, physical, and ethical dimensions. 

HCI and embodied design emphasize that digital systems are experienced through bodies, behaviors, environments, and social systems, not in isolation. Embodied design illustrates how integrating bodily experience into digital applications can enhance learning and interaction \cite{wilde2015}.

I believe design should act as a critical mediator between technological possibility and human reality. Rather than asking what can be built, designers should ask what should be built, for whom, and under which conditions. Technology is not inherently meaningful; its value emerges only when it is carefully situated within context and aligned with human needs. I want to see the world become more balanced in its application of technology, and how it can enrich for example education \cite{bakker2010}.

I am particularly drawn to this intersection between technological systems and physical engagement. Designing within this space requires both technical proficiency and a human-centered mindset, empathy, systems awareness, and the ability to critically evaluate when technology enhances an experience or when restraint and physical alternatives may be more appropriate. Responsible design is therefore not about maximizing technological presence, but about intentional integration.
